opus-5.5.text:
I think abstractions are going to be really central, and honestly that's been one of the big shifts in how I think about this work over the last few years.

When we did the original FlashAttention, a lot of it was written pretty close to the metal. You're thinking about shared memory, about registers, about how threads in a warp are laid out, and you're hand-tuning a lot of that. That works, and you can get great performance, but it doesn't scale very well in terms of human effort. Every time a new chip comes out, Hopper, then Blackwell, or a different vendor like AMD, or some of the newer accelerators, you basically have to redo a big chunk of that work. And there just aren't that many people in the world who can write those kernels.

So the question becomes: what's the right level of abstraction where you can still express the things that matter for performance, like tiling, data movement between levels of the memory hierarchy, overlapping compute with memory loads, but without having to manage every single detail by hand? Things like CUTLASS and CuTe, and more recently Triton and some of the newer DSLs, are trying to hit that sweet spot. With CuTe, for example, the layout abstraction lets you reason about how data is partitioned across threads and how it maps to the tensor cores in a much cleaner way. That made writing FlashAttention-2 and -3 a lot more manageable than it would have been otherwise.

I think the interesting thing is that the core ideas tend to be pretty stable across hardware. You almost always care about the memory hierarchy, you want to keep data in fast memory as long as possible, you want to feed the matrix multiply units, and you want asynchrony so that you're not stalling. The specific instructions change, but those principles don't. So if you can build abstractions around those principles, you get a lot more portability, and you can let compilers or autotuners handle the hardware-specific parts.

There's always a tension, though. The abstraction has to be leaky in the right places. If it hides too much, you lose the last 20 or 30 percent of performance, and in this field that 20 or 30 percent matters a lot when you're spending hundreds of millions of dollars on compute. So I think the best abstractions are the ones that give you a productive default but still let an expert drop down a level when they need to.

And longer term, I'm pretty excited about the idea that these abstractions also make the problem more amenable to automation, whether that's better compilers or even using models themselves to help generate and optimize kernels. If you have a well-structured search space, it's much easier for an automated system to explore it than if everything is raw assembly. So I see abstractions as the thing that lets this kind of optimization work go from a handful of specialists to something much broader.

r001.rationale: The response says abstractions can make optimization work more manageable and accessible beyond a handful of specialists, but it does not identify faster productivity for newly hired engineers.

r002.rationale: The response says well-structured abstractions can make kernel generation and optimization more amenable to automation, including using models to help.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think abstractions are really the whole game right now, honestly. If you look at what we've been doing with FlashAttention over the past few years, each version was essentially a hand-crafted kernel for a specific generation of hardware. FlashAttention-2 for Ampere, FlashAttention-3 for Hopper, and you have to rewrite a huge amount when the hardware changes. The hardware is moving so fast, every year or two there's a new generation with new instructions, new memory hierarchy, new ways to move data around, and the kernels you wrote don't automatically take advantage of that. So the question is: how do you not redo all of that work every single time?

The way I think about it is there are really a few layers. At the bottom you have the hardware itself, and the vendors expose that through very low-level primitives, like CUTLASS and CuTe on the NVIDIA side. Those are very powerful but also very painful. You're thinking about tensor layouts, swizzling, how warps are mapped to tiles, all of that. Above that you have things like Triton, which is a really nice abstraction where you're writing at the block level, you don't think about individual threads, and the compiler handles a lot of the scheduling. And then at the top you have PyTorch and torch.compile, where most people actually live.

What I've found is that no single layer is right for everything. For the really performance-critical pieces, attention, matmul, the stuff that's eighty or ninety percent of the FLOPs, you still often want to go down pretty close to the metal, because the compilers haven't quite caught up to what a human expert can do, especially on the newest hardware. But that's a tiny fraction of the code. For everything else, the normalization layers, the activation functions, the glue, you absolutely want something like Triton or torch.compile, because the productivity gain is enormous and you're within ten or twenty percent of hand-tuned anyway.

The thing I'm excited about is pushing the boundary of what the higher-level abstractions can express. There's a lot of work now on things like ThunderKittens, on CuTe DSL in Python, on Triton getting better support for things like warp specialization and async pipelining, where you're trying to expose the hardware's capabilities, the TMA, the asynchronous tensor core instructions, without forcing people to write a thousand lines of C++ templates. If you can get the right abstraction, where the expert can still express the tricks they know, but the code is five times shorter and portable across generations, that's a huge win.

And then the other piece is, with other accelerators, with AMD, with TPUs, with all these new chips, the abstraction question becomes even more important, because you really can't afford to hand-write everything for every piece of hardware. The dream is that you write the algorithm once at a fairly high level, say what you want in terms of data movement and tiling, and the lower layers figure out the mapping. We're not fully there, but I think we're a lot closer than we were two or three years ago, and I think a lot of that is going to be driven by the fact that the models themselves are now helping write these kernels. That changes the calculus a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says higher-level abstractions can improve productivity, but does not connect that benefit to newly hired engineers.

r002.rationale: It says models are helping write kernels, but does not propose designing abstractions specifically to enable AI to perform hardware optimization work.

astra-6.text:
I think abstractions are essential, because you can’t expect everyone working on a model to understand every detail of the hardware. But the abstraction has to expose the things that matter for performance. For GPUs, that often means data movement: what lives in registers, what lives in shared memory, and when you have to go back to high-bandwidth memory.

FlashAttention is one example of that. At the model level, you still have attention. Underneath, you can change how you tile the computation and schedule the work to avoid materializing a large intermediate matrix. You preserve the interface while making the implementation much more efficient.

The challenge across accelerators is that a clean interface doesn’t automatically give you performance portability. Different hardware needs different choices underneath. So I’d like abstractions that let us express the algorithm and its data movement clearly, while giving a compiler or a hardware-specific implementation room to choose the right layout and schedule. That’s how optimization work becomes reusable, instead of everyone having to start from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says abstractions let model developers avoid learning every hardware detail and make optimization reusable, but it does not identify faster onboarding or productivity for newly hired engineers.

r002.rationale: The response gives compilers or hardware-specific implementations room to choose layouts and schedules, but does not propose enabling AI to perform hardware optimization work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think abstractions are really important because we can’t expect everyone to become an expert in every GPU architecture. Ideally, you can express what you want to compute at a fairly high level, and the compiler or the library takes care of mapping that onto the hardware efficiently.

The challenge is choosing what to hide. If an abstraction hides data movement completely, for example, it can make it difficult to understand why something is slow or how to improve it. For a lot of these workloads, where the data lives and how you move it are as important as the arithmetic.

So I’d like abstractions that let you express the algorithm clearly, but also give you control over things like tiling and memory layout when you need it. Then you can reuse the algorithm across accelerators while specializing the pieces that depend on the hardware. You still need people doing low-level optimization, but their work can become something that many more people build on.

r001.rationale: The response says abstractions let people avoid becoming experts in every GPU architecture, but it does not mention newly hired engineers or making them productive more quickly.

r002.rationale: The response discusses compilers and libraries mapping computations to hardware, but does not propose enabling AI to perform hardware optimization work.
